title: Explain polymorphism (compile-time overloading vs runtime overriding) with examples and why it is useful.
shortTitle: What is polymorphism and why is it useful?

s1_definition.profdef: Polymorphism means "many forms" — one interface, multiple implementations. Two types: COMPILE-TIME (method overloading — same name, different parameters, compiler picks) and RUNTIME (method overriding — same signature in parent/child, JVM picks based on actual object type). WHY it's useful: (1) WRITE GENERIC CODE that works with any subtype — one loop processes SavingsAccount, CurrentAccount, NRIAccount without knowing the specific type. (2) OPEN/CLOSED PRINCIPLE — add new types WITHOUT modifying existing code. (3) STRATEGY PATTERN — swap behavior at runtime by injecting different implementations. (4) ELIMINATE if-else/switch CHAINS — instead of `if (type == "SAVINGS") { ... } else if (type == "CURRENT") { ... }`, let polymorphism dispatch automatically. In production banking systems, polymorphism reduces code from 500 lines of if-else to 50 lines of polymorphic method calls.
s1_definition.analogy: The bank's notification system needs to send messages: SMS for savings customers, email for premium customers, push notification for mobile customers. WITHOUT polymorphism: `if (type == "SMS") sendSms(); else if (type == "EMAIL") sendEmail(); else if (type == "PUSH") sendPush();` — grows with every new channel. WITH polymorphism: `notificationChannel.send(message)` — ONE call. The JVM picks the right implementation at runtime. Adding WhatsApp channel: create `WhatsAppChannel implements NotificationChannel` — ZERO changes to existing code.
s1_definition.oneliner: Polymorphism = one call, many behaviors. Compile-time: overloading (compiler picks by args). Runtime: overriding (JVM picks by actual type). Useful: eliminates if-else chains, enables Open/Closed Principle, powers Strategy pattern.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Polymorphism means "many forms" — one interface, multiple implementations. Two types: COMPILE-TIME (method overloading — same name, different parameters, compiler picks) and RUNTIME (method overriding — same signature in parent/child, JVM picks based on actual object type). WHY it's useful: (1) WRITE GENERIC CODE that works with any subtype — one loop processes SavingsAccount, CurrentAccount, NRIAccount without knowing the specific type. (2) OPEN/CLOSED PRINCIPLE — add new types WITHOUT modifying existing code. (3) STRATEGY PATTERN — swap behavior at runtime by injecting different implementations. (4) ELIMINATE if-else/switch CHAINS — instead of `if (type == "SAVINGS") { ... } else if (type == "CURRENT") { ... }`, let polymorphism dispatch automatically. In production banking systems, polymorphism reduces code from 500 lines of if-else to 50 lines of polymorphic method calls.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The bank's notification system needs to send messages: SMS for savings customers, email for premium customers, push notification for mobile customers. WITHOUT polymorphism: `if (type == "SMS") sendSms(); else if (type == "EMAIL") sendEmail(); else if (type == "PUSH") sendPush();` — grows with every new channel. WITH polymorphism: `notificationChannel.send(message)` — ONE call. The JVM picks the right implementation at runtime. Adding WhatsApp channel: create `WhatsAppChannel implements NotificationChannel` — ZERO changes to existing code.

**One line to remember:** Polymorphism = one call, many behaviors. Compile-time: overloading (compiler picks by args). Runtime: overriding (JVM picks by actual type). Useful: eliminates if-else chains, enables Open/Closed Principle, powers Strategy pattern.

sections.s3_banking:
**Problem — The bank's notification system sends messages through multiple channels.** The old code had a 200-line switch statement: `switch(channelType) { case "SMS": ... case "EMAIL": ... case "PUSH": ... }`. Every new channel (WhatsApp, in-app, voice call) required modifying the switch. Bug rate increased with each addition. The team refactors to polymorphism: `NotificationChannel` interface with `send(message)` method. Each channel implements its own `send()`. The dispatcher calls `channel.send(message)` — one line, no switch. Adding WhatsApp: create class, implement interface. ZERO changes to dispatcher.

**What the project will show:** Interface-based runtime polymorphism replacing a switch statement, Strategy pattern for fee calculation, generic processing loop, adding a new channel with zero modification to existing code, compile-time polymorphism (overloaded send methods), and the Open/Closed Principle proven by test.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** Spring injects all 4 NotificationChannel beans into NotificationDispatcher as `List<NotificationChannel>`. Each is a different implementation — but the dispatcher sees them as the SAME interface.

**Step 2.** `sendVia("SMS", phone, message)` finds SmsChannel from the list. Calls `channel.send(phone, message)`. JVM dispatches to SmsChannel.send() — truncates to 160 chars, calls SMS gateway.

**Step 3.** `sendVia("EMAIL", email, message)` finds EmailChannel. SAME `channel.send()` call. JVM dispatches to EmailChannel.send() — HTML formatting, SMTP. SAME code path in dispatcher, DIFFERENT behavior.

**Step 4.** `broadcast(recipient, message)` loops ALL channels. ONE loop, FOUR different behaviors. No if-else. Each channel's send() does its own thing — SMS truncates, email formats HTML, push sends to Firebase, WhatsApp uses Business API.

**Step 5.** 6 months later: WhatsApp channel added. Create WhatsAppChannel.java, register as @Bean. NotificationDispatcher: ZERO changes. SmsChannel/EmailChannel/PushChannel: ZERO changes. Tests for existing channels: STILL PASS. Open/Closed Principle in action.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ POLYMORPHISM — ONE CALL, MANY BEHAVIORS ═══

  dispatcher.sendVia("SMS", phone, msg)
    → channel.send(phone, msg)
    → JVM: actual type = SmsChannel → SmsChannel.send() → truncate + SMS gateway

  dispatcher.sendVia("EMAIL", email, msg)
    → channel.send(email, msg)
    → JVM: actual type = EmailChannel → EmailChannel.send() → HTML + SMTP

  SAME method call. DIFFERENT implementations. JVM dispatches at RUNTIME.

  ═══ WHY POLYMORPHISM IS USEFUL ═══

  1. ELIMINATES IF-ELSE:
     (Avoid) if (type=="SMS") sendSms(); else if (type=="EMAIL") sendEmail(); ...
     (Recommended) channel.send(msg);  — ONE line, JVM dispatches

  2. OPEN/CLOSED PRINCIPLE:
     Add WhatsAppChannel → ZERO changes to dispatcher
     Add VoiceChannel → ZERO changes to dispatcher

  3. STRATEGY PATTERN:
     Inject different InterestStrategy → different behavior at runtime
     Switch strategy via config — no code change

  4. GENERIC PROCESSING:
     for (Channel ch : allChannels) { ch.send(msg); }
     ONE loop. N different behaviors. Fully extensible.
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Polymorphism means "many forms" — one interface, multiple implementations. Compile-time polymorphism is method overloading: same name, different parameters, compiler picks. Runtime polymorphism is method overriding: same signature, different classes, JVM picks based on actual object type. Runtime polymorphism is the more powerful form because it enables four critical production benefits: eliminating growing if-else/switch chains, Open/Closed Principle (add types without modifying existing code), Strategy pattern (swap behavior at runtime via injection), and generic processing (one loop handles all types).

In my notification dispatch service, `channel.send(recipient, message)` dispatches to SmsChannel, EmailChannel, PushChannel, or WhatsAppChannel at runtime — one line replaces a 200-line switch statement. When WhatsApp was added 6 months later: one new class implementing the interface, one @Bean registration. NotificationDispatcher: zero lines changed. Existing channels: zero lines changed. Existing tests: still pass. This is the Open/Closed Principle powered by runtime polymorphism.

The practical test of polymorphism understanding is: can you ADD a new type without MODIFYING existing code? In my dispatcher, adding VoiceCallChannel requires: create class, implement NotificationChannel, register as bean. The dispatcher, existing channels, and existing tests are UNTOUCHED. If your design requires modifying a switch statement or if-else chain to add a new type, you're not using polymorphism correctly. The interview answer: "polymorphism eliminates conditional logic and enables extension without modification."
